lines.text: You know exactly what the agent should do next. Writing it down is the slow part: a title, a paragraph, the same instructions as yesterday.
Then you press send, spot the typo a second later, and the agent has already read it, with the last task still in its head.
Agent R Q makes handing off work fast. Talk instead of type, skip the title, reuse what you always say, take a message back, and start every task clean.
Naming a task often takes longer than writing it.
Ada presses N, anywhere in the app, and the new task form opens for storefront.
The title is optional, so she writes only the task: after a coupon is removed, the checkout still shows the discounted price.
Command Enter creates it. For a moment, it is called Untitled.
Then a small model, running right in her browser, reads the description and gives the task a name. Nothing is sent anywhere to write it.
Want the title before you create? Type a few words, and click the sparkle beside the title field.
Some tasks take a whole paragraph. Typing it is the slow part.
So Ada clicks the mic in the reply box, and just says it.
The first time, a Whisper speech model downloads into her browser. After that, it's ready.
When she stops, the text lands where her cursor was. On a computer, her voice becomes text on her own machine, and no audio is uploaded.
She picks the language she speaks in Settings, under Input. On a phone, the mic uses the phone's own dictation.
Some instructions you type every single day: pull the latest main, run the tests, tag and push.
Ada saves it once, as a preset: in the workspace settings, a short name, the message, and Add Preset.
Now, in any task or reply, she types a hash and the first letters of the name, and picks it from the menu.
The name becomes the whole message, right where she typed it. The agent just reads the message, so there's nothing to set up on its side.
You press send, and see the mistake one second later. Too late: the agent read it.
In Agent R Q, a reply waits a few seconds before it goes: Sending in five seconds, with Cancel and Send Now.
Cancel puts the message back in the box, unsent, attachments and all. Ada fixes the branch name.
Send Now delivers it at once. Leave it alone, and it goes when the count reaches zero.
Each workspace sets its own delay, from off to sixty seconds. New workspaces start at five.
Four workspaces, dozens of tasks. Finding the one you need shouldn't be a hunt.
Command K opens the task finder. Ada types coupon, a word from the description, and it finds the task. It searches every task this device has opened, and Enter opens it.
Single letters do the rest: N for a new task, W to switch workspace, M for a machine, and P for the Panno.
Inside a task, C shows the chat, and T shows the agent's tool calls.
A question mark lists them all. They pause while you type in a field, so they never get in your way.
An agent that runs all day starts your third task with the first two still in its context, and reads them again on every turn.
Storefront's Claude Code runs on Ada's machine, so the new task form shows an eraser next to YOLO: clear context.
Before the agent picks the task up, Agent R Q types slash clear into its terminal, waits two seconds, then hands the task over.
In the live terminal you can watch it happen: the context clears, and the new task arrives on a clean slate.
It's on by default for new workspaces, in the Automations settings. Agents can ask for it too, when they create a task.
Skip the title, say it out loud, reuse what you always type, take a message back, find anything with a key, and start each task clean.
What slows down your handoffs today? Tell us in the comments, and try it at Agent R Q dot com.
